en: Itivuttaka 99: Tikanipāta, Pañcamavagga Thus it was said. This discourse was spoken by the Blessed One while staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Having understood the meaning, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these verses: “Those who have abandoned the three things, And have fully understood the three things, Having cut off craving for the three things, They do not come again to this world. “What are the three things that have been abandoned? Greed, hatred, and delusion—these are the three things that have been abandoned. “And what are the three things that have been fully understood? Suffering, its origin, and its cessation—these are the three things that have been fully understood. “And what are the three things for which craving has been cut off? The eye, forms, and eye-consciousness; the ear, sounds, and ear-consciousness; the nose, odors, and nose-consciousness; the tongue, tastes, and tongue-consciousness; the body, tangibles, and body-consciousness; the mind, mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness—these are the three things for which craving has been cut off. “Those who have abandoned these three things, And have fully understood these three things, Having cut off craving for these three things, They do not come again to this world. This is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Having heard the Venerable Ānanda’s words, those monks were satisfied and rejoiced in his speech. Thus ends the ninety-ninth discourse, “The Threefold,” in the Fifth Chapter of the Section on Threes.
The Discourse on the Threefold Knowledge.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard:
"Monks, it is by way of the Dhamma that I describe a brahmin as possessing the threefold knowledge, and not merely by means of reciting and rehearsing."
And how, monks, do I describe a brahmin who possesses the threefold knowledge according to the Dhamma, and not merely by means of reciting and rehearsing?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births...
"Thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births;
many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion:
'There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.'"
"Passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere. There too, I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.
Passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.

This is the first true knowledge (vijjā) attained by him; ignorance is destroyed and true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled and light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
Furthermore, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, a monk sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.

He understands beings as they fare according to their karma: "These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have gone to a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a world of ruin."

‘...have been reborn in hell. Or else: ‘These worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view—these, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye...
With the pure divine eye, surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate;
he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

This is the second true knowledge attained by him: ignorance is destroyed, true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled, light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

Furthermore, monks, with the destruction of the taints, a monk dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, entering upon and abiding therein.

This is the third true knowledge attained by him; ignorance is dispelled and true knowledge has arisen; darkness is dispelled and light has arisen, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
It is in this way, monks, that I describe a brahmin as "thrice-learned" according to the Dhamma, and not merely by the measure of reciting and rehearsing texts.
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“He recollects his former abodes...”
He beholds both heaven and the states of woe;
moreover, having reached the destruction of birth,
the sage is perfected through direct knowledge.
By means of these three knowledges,
a brahmin becomes one who possesses the threefold knowledge;
him I call one who possesses the threefold knowledge.
“Nor is it anything else but mere chatter.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The tenth [sutta].
The Fifth Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Clarity, life, and the outer robe;
Through investigation of the fire;
rebirth, lovely things, and merit—
these ten are for you through giving according to the Dhamma.
The Third Chapter is concluded.
